cases.query: what is the monitoring used for lithium

sources.title: Lithium(CAMHS)
sources.content:
Lithium
MONITORING
Baseline Tests1
• Full Blood Picture
• Urea and Electrolytes
• Renal function
• Calcium levels
• Thyroid Function Test (TFT): TSH and T4
• Parathyroid hormone concentrations
• Weight or body mass index (BMI)
• ECG – in those with risk factors for or existing/family history of cardiovascular disease.
After commencing lithium, check weight, serum calcium (including ionised calcium) and
parathyroid hormone concentrations, and renal and thyroid function every 3–6 months (at least
annually), or as clinically indicated.

Serum Lithium Levels
Therapeutic level for treatment:
• Acute mania 0.6–1 mmol/L1,2
• Depression: 0.4–0.6 mmol/L5
Therapeutic level for prophylaxis:
• 0.4–0.8 mmol/L1,5

Serum lithium concentrations tend to fluctuate for 6–10 hours after dosing, so the 12-hour
post-dose serum concentration is used for monitoring purposes.1, 5

Check serum lithium levels 5–7 days after starting treatment and after each dose change until
stabilised. Steady state may not be reached for 4–7 days (longer in those with renal impairment).1

Once stable, serum lithium concentrations should be monitored once every three months.1

sources.content:

Monitoring of lithium is particularly complex, given its narrow therapeutic index, and propensity for dose-
related side effects and for serious interactions with other medications. Regular measurement of plasma
lithium levels is required, with increased frequency of monitoring needed during treatment initiation and
dose titration/reduction.[29] Service arrangements vary, but in practice responsibility for monitoring
may be shared between primary and secondary care. It is strongly advisable that primary care centers
responsible for monitoring lithium levels have a robust call/recall safety netting system in place, e.g., with
a monthly computerised search of the electronic patient record, and regular review dates for prescriptions.
For many patients, ongoing monitoring/management of substance use is an essential component of long-
term bipolar management, with appropriate referral as indicated.[298]

sources.title: Lithium Clinical Guideline(EMHS)
sources.content:
Frequency of monitoring
It is recommended that lithium levels be checked by nursing/medical staff as follows:
• On admission to hospital for patients on lithium
• Following initiation – 5 to 7 days after commencing treatment, then once weekly for
the first four weeks (for inpatients)
• After each dose change – check level at 5 to 7 days post dose change
• While on maintenance - every 3 months after a stable therapeutic concentration has
been achieved
• More frequent monitoring is recommended when there are:
o Changes in
• fluid intake or signs of illness which may impact fluid balance
• diet – in particular where there is an increase in sodium intake
• mental state
o Concurrent use of interacting medications. Refer to Medication interactions
o Signs and symptoms of possible lithium toxicity. Refer to Lithium toxicity in the
Adverse effects section.
Nursing staff are to record observations on the Lithium Monitoring Form as directed and
notify the prescriber of any abnormal reading. The MO is to:
• Complete timely, ongoing assessment of required monitoring parameters
• Devise a monitoring plan to ensure the patient’s ongoing care is comprehensively
understood by the entire care team.

sources.title: Lithium Therapy - Initiation And Continuation Guideline(FSH)
sources.content:
OFFICIAL
Lithium Therapy - Initiation and Continuation

o Increase daily dose in 225 to 450mg increments based on serum lithium
levels (refer to section 1.9 Therapeutic Drug monitoring)

o A daily dose of 900 to 2250mg is usually required, except in elderly who
may require a third to half this dose due to poor tolerability

• Prophylaxis of bipolar disorder:

o IR product: 250 to 1000mg daily in 2 or 3 divided doses or as a single
dose at night

o Increase daily dose in 250 to 500mg increments based on serum lithium
levels (refer to section 1.9 Therapeutic Drug monitoring)

o SR product: 450 to 675mg daily in 2 divided doses or as a single dose at
night

o Increase daily dose in 225 to 450mg increments based on serum lithium
levels (refer to section 1.9 Therapeutic Drug monitoring)

2.8. Therapeutic Drug Monitoring
• Blood taken for serum lithium levels should be taken 12 hours after the last
dose. Doses that would be given prior to blood being drawn should be
withheld until after blood has been taken.

• Steady state concentration is achieved after 5-7 days. This may be longer
(between 7-10 days) in the elderly or those with renal impairment.

• Levels should be assessed:

sources.title: Lithium Therapy - Initiation And Continuation Guideline(FSH)
sources.content:
OFFICIAL
Lithium Therapy - Initiation and Continuation

• NSAIDs: (e.g. ibuprofen) can reduce lithium clearance and therefore
increase lithium levels and the risk of toxicity. Avoid the combination where
possible. Low dose aspirin is safe to use.

• Serotonergic drugs: Lithium can contribute to serotonin toxicity, therefore
patients who are prescribed combinations of serotonergic drugs should be
closely monitored

• Anti-psychotics: rapid dose increases of lithium and antipsychotics together
may cause neurotoxicity.

• Urinary alkaliniser’s: (e.g. sodium bicarbonate and potassium citrate (found
in cystitis-relief sachets and some antacids) can theoretically increase lithium
clearance and thereby reduce efficacy. However, it is likely that high doses
would need to be consumed to have a significant effect.

2.7. Dosage (as lithium carbonate)
• Doses should be individualised depending on indication and patient risk
factors i.e. weight, comorbidities (e.g. renal impairment) and concomitant
medications, and titrated based on serum lithium levels (refer to section 1.9.
Therapeutic Drug Monitoring), tolerability and clinical response.

• The total daily dose of lithium should not exceed 2500mg.

Target levels and dose adjustments
Refer also to information on usual therapeutic ranges outlined on the RPBG Lithium
Monitoring Form.
• Acute mania
o Target serum level: 0.8-1.2 mmol/L.
o Once remission occurs (7-14 days), gradually decrease to maintenance dose, aim
for BPAD prophylaxis lithium levels (below).
• BPAD prophylaxis
o Target serum level: 0.4-1 mmol/L (0.6-0.8 mmol/L if BPAD stabilised).
o Dosage will vary from one individual to another. Usual maintenance dose is in
between 250 mg to 1200 mg daily.
• Augmentation of antidepressant therapy
o Target serum level: 0.6-1 mmol/L.
• Older adult
o Target serum level: 0.4-0.7 mmol/L.
• Special considerations
o Reduce dose and monitor more closely in patients with renal impairment.
o Where serum creatinine levels are observed to be rising, and decreased creatinine
clearance/acute renal impairment is suspected, seek expert advice (contact Renal
Physician).

sources.title: High Risk Medicines(CAMHS)
sources.content:
is important to frequently monitor patient parameters
including renal function, thyroid function, urea and
electrolytes and lithium levels to ensure toxicity does not
eventuate.4

The most significant contributors to lithium toxicity are4:

• interactions with drugs that affect renal function (e.g.
diuretics, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs),
angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors or
angiotensin II receptor blockers)

• reduced fluid or salt intake

• fluid loss from vomiting, diarrhoea or excessive sweating.

Toxicity may also be caused by deliberate or inadvertent
overdose.

Lithium is available in 250 mg immediate release tablets and
450 mg (scored) controlled release tablets. All medication
orders should clearly state the formulation as the
pharmacokinetics of these products are vastly different.

Adverse effects
Lithium toxicity
1,2,3
The typical signs and symptoms associated with lithium toxicity varies dependent on
serum lithium levels.
• Signs and symptoms of mild to moderate toxicity:
o Drowsiness, blurred vision, increasing diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, anorexia,
muscle weakness, drowsiness, apathy, ataxia, flu-like illness.
• Signs and symptoms of severe toxicity:
o Increased muscle tone, hyperreflexia, myoclonic jerks, coarse tremor, dysarthria,
disorientation, psychosis, seizures, coma, QT-interval prolongation and death.
Escalation of care
Where a patient demonstrates signs and symptoms of toxicity (i.e. mild,
moderate or severe), complete the following:
1. Nurse, Pharmacist or Medical Officer (MO) to withhold lithium (noting “W” on WA
Hospital Medication Chart [HMC]).
2. MO to check the serum lithium level (note time of last dose) and renal function as
soon as possible from the time of escalation.
